text: You now have three different ways to picture the same quantum state. This lab is about building the judgment to pick the right one for the right audience — a skill that matters as much as knowing the plotting calls themselves.

Reuse the Bell-state circuit from this chapter. plot_histogram on the real seeded counts renders two bars, 00 and 11, each near the chart's mid-height, with no bars at all for 01 or 10. This is a measurement-outcome picture: what came out of actually running the circuit N times, nothing more and nothing less.

Here's the part that matters most in this lab. Attempting a Bloch sphere on this entangled circuit still produces some picture — one small sphere per qubit — but it's misleading. Each qubit's own reduced state, when entangled with the other, is a maximally mixed state: 50/50 outcome probability, no definite phase to point to. Geometrically, a maximally mixed state sits at the exact center of the sphere, not on its surface, because it's an equal mixture of every pure state. A per-qubit Bloch sphere on an entangled state looks like it's showing you something, but what it's actually showing is the absence of any definite single-qubit state to point to.

The Q-sphere is where the entanglement actually shows up: exactly two blobs, at 00 and 11, equal in size and equal in color, with nothing at 01 or 10. Unlike the Bloch sphere attempt, this picture directly shows which basis states participate, with what relative weight, and with what relative phase.

For a non-technical stakeholder who wants to know whether the quantum computer did the thing you expected, the histogram is almost always right — it maps directly onto a question they already understand, no need to explain phase or superposition first. For a fellow quantum engineer debugging circuit behavior, the Q-sphere is usually more useful, because it shows the relative phase a histogram simply cannot — a circuit subtly wrong in a way that flips phase but leaves probabilities identical would look unchanged on a histogram but show up immediately on a Q-sphere. The Bloch sphere, despite being the most familiar of the three, is the wrong tool here specifically because this state is entangled.
